#20208. As an Awkward Teen, Grand Theft Auto Was My Escape. Now It Feels Like Real Life.

As an Awkward Teen, Grand Theft Auto Was My Escape. Now It Feels Like Real Life.

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1697 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that this morning, I woke up at 7:00 AM to play Grand Theft Auto VI just hours after its release.
  • Grand Theft Auto, first released in 1997, and GTA 2, which followed two years later, were top-down driving games whose mechanics and visuals never intrigued me as a child.
  • I don’t remember much about that particular ThesFest, but I do remember being grateful for Zack or Zach’s generosity.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that this morning, I woke up at 7:00 AM to play Grand Theft Auto VI just hours after its release. It’s the first fresh installment of the franchise since 2013; the one whose first trailer was released three years ago; the one that probably cost over a billion dollars to produce; the one set in a satirical, fictionalized south Florida; the one described in this very magazine as “the peak of entertainment.” During my first four hours with the game, I made a few hundred dollars doing odd jobs, performed several repairs on my swamp-front fixer-upper, knocked out a few sets of kettlebell swings on the deck, did favors for two friendly neighbors, and ran a mile to retrieve a freshly repainted car I left behind at a fishing spot just outside of town. I’m writing in vague terms not only to avoid spoiling the game’s plot but because, so far, it hasn’t been all that exciting. The absurd and hyperrealistic mundanity of its gameplay is, simply, astonishing, and more than I ever could have wanted from a franchise I’ve been playing for nearly a quarter of a century.

Grand Theft Auto, first released in 1997, and GTA 2, which followed two years later, were top-down driving games whose mechanics and visuals never intrigued me as a child. I wasn’t even aware of their existence until learning of the franchise’s third entry, and the first in 3D. I discovered GTA in a hotel room in Wichita Falls, TX, a small city just a stone’s throw from Oklahoma, because a classmate named Zach (or Zack) risked damaging his PS2 by toting it along on a school trip. We were there for the annual Texas Thespian Festival, an opportunity for dramatically inclined teenagers to perform plays and musicals in front of strange kids from strange schools and compete for prizes that, like most awards, quickly lost meaning after they were bestowed. After attending the required main stage productions, many of which were watered down to their school-friendly “Junior” adaptations—Into the Woods without the second act deaths and darkness, Guys & Dolls with considerably less gambling—we returned to the nearby hotel where students slept three to a room and were told to behave. For several nights we took turns playing this impossibly violent and vulgar game, five or six of us huddled around the television parked on a dresser no one used. We stole cars, killed non-player characters with assault rifles, and even completed an occasional story mission, most of which required, well, stealing cars and killing non-player characters with assault rifles. We were actors, and wasn’t gaming just another form of performance?

I don’t remember much about that particular ThesFest, but I do remember being grateful for Zack or Zach’s generosity. Before that moment, he was simply an intimidatingly charming and friendly older boy I knew best for playing Romeo in a production that our school’s theater director chose to set during the Vietnam War for reasons he was unable to articulate. (In that, my first stage role, I was cast as Juliet’s unnamed little brother, a role that doesn’t exist in the original text.) Of course I’d played video games before that weekend—Myst, Rollercoaster Tycoon and a Titanic-themed mystery were my favorites at that point—but never before had I experienced something so immersive or graphically impressive. It was loud and exciting, a simulation of real life at its most extreme and chaotic. When I got home, I knew the console–and GTA 3–had to be mine. My life, laser-focused on math homework and our theater director’s post-apocalyptic interpretation of Antigone, could have really used a thrill.

Industry observers note that I traded in my PlayStation, a Christmas gift from years earlier on which I played mostly rented or borrowed adventure games, and used money I’d saved from mowing lawns (my family’s own, and those of a few elderly neighbors), to pay the balance. The only game I wanted was GTA III, and it’s the only one I played for months. The novelty was the thing. There was a story, of course: some nameless protagonist with a chiseled, low-polygon face committing crimes and various acts of violence to achieve a goal of… staying alive? Perhaps that’s the goal of most games, maybe even the goal of life itself. I skipped cutscenes in favor of driving from one glowing cylindrical marker to the next, shooting police officers in the head and picking up sex workers who did unseen, noisy things to my character that made the stolen cars bounce up and down like a lowrider with hydraulics. I’d largely missed the groundbreaking graphics of the N64 era—having never played Zelda or Mario Kart or GoldenEye outside the bedrooms of childhood friends with bigger houses and never-ending supplies of soda in the fridge—which meant my first truly passionate dive into console gaming was filled with manic, gratuitous violence. The original PlayStation was for catching troublemaking monkeys in nets and flying around gentle landscapes as a purple dragon. The PS2, though, was for imagining a life of crime. That my parents allowed me to play these games at all still surprises me, but I suppose to them anything was better than me getting drunk at parties I knew were happening but was never invited to.

Recent findings suggest that by the time Grand Theft Auto: Vice City was released the following year, I had a part time job at a local AMC, so I bought the game with money earned selling popcorn and cleaning that same popcorn off the floor. Playing it was a reward for completing an essay on Ernest Hemingway or telling multiple moviegoers that we couldn’t give refunds simply because they “didn’t like” Men In Black 2. The game’s soundtrack introduced me to songs that still activate memories sitting cross-legged on the carpet of my bedroom, turning the volume down as low as I could to prevent my father from stepping inside and saying, gravely, “Am I going to have to turn that off?” To this day, I can’t hear Laura Branagin’s “Self Control” without conjuring Tommy Vercetti, the protagonist of Grand Theft Auto: Vice City, driving a motorcycle down a sparsely populated road flanked by neon-lit palm trees. For months, I listened to more in-game radio than the local Top 40 station, unaware at the time that its curated period playlists would shape my musical appetite for the rest of my life.

According to recent reports, the third installment of that PS2 trilogy, Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas, came out two years later, when I was a freshman in college. I was 18, adjusting to life in a new city, and trying desperately to make friends. The game was less a reward for hard work than a balm when I didn’t feel like socializing, a distraction from my countless first semester anxieties. By the time I completed its main story, life away from home had become normal. I had new friends, new obligations, new problems. I used my PS2 as a DVD player almost exclusively, watching several movies a week, all borrowed from Netflix (during its original red-envelope form) and the school library. By the time GTA 4 was released, I’d lost interest in gaming altogether. We were in a recession, and I was hellbent on keeping my very first real job. In fact, I didn’t play another Grand Theft Auto game until 2013, on a PS3 Slim (the console’s discounted, late-generation entry), weeks after my now-husband and I moved into our first apartment together. In the time since my last GTA experience, I’d come out of the closet, moved across the country, started a new career, adopted my first cat, and made an entirely new group of close friends. A franchise that was once a distraction from teenage malaise was now pure, unadulterated fun. Gone were the days of playing it at a low volume–I turned it all the way up, and didn’t skip cut scenes. I was there for the story as well as the spectacle.

13 years later, the longest ever interval between new installments, my relationship with gaming has evolved alongside the games themselves. It’s not enough to be distracted; being distracted is now our default state. Disturbances arise, whether seeking them or not: a text message in the middle of a terrible Peacock show; a news alert regarding a global calamity about which you can do nothing but panic; the jittering beeps of FaceTime call while reading a wonderful novel, or that mindless, habitual scroll through a feed that indicates videos meant to be seen but not remembered. Lately I’ve turned to gaming for total immersion, for sensations of genuine awe that might keep me from succumbing to the dopamine rush of my phone. I spent much of the summer replaying Kingdom Come Deliverance and its sequel, a pair of life simulators set in medieval Europe. In those games, every action has a consequence, and every success is hard-fought and requires patience.

Industry observers note that after several hours in its impossibly dense world, GTA 6 seems to be encouraging a similar sense of duty. My real life is fine, often even good. It’s the kind of life I thought impossible when the franchise first entered my life nearly a quarter century ago. I’m not bowled over by the game because it’s better or even more fun than the life I live outside Vice City—there are gun-toting mass murderers in both, after all—but because it’s totally different. Even when you’re comfortable in your own life, isn’t it extraordinary to enter another? The games have always been about adults, and for adults. It states so right on the box. Since 2002, their goals have fundamentally remained the same: get a job, make money, stay alive. As a teenager, its simulated depravity was funny and exciting, with graphics and gameplay so vivid I could feel like a kid again. But now, at 40? With 20-plus years of GTA under my belt and a life 16-year-old me would find more unbelievable than the functionalities of the PS5 Pro? No game has ever made me feel older. What a privilege that is.

Best-Ever Pavlova

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Pavlova is essentially a massive meringue that melts in your mouth.
  • If you’re looking for something a bit more festive, check out our Christmas wreath pavlova for a holiday spin on the classic.
  • Arrange a rack in the center of the oven; preheat to 300°.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pavlova is essentially a massive meringue that melts in your mouth. We top our version with whipped cream and fresh berries for an airy and fruity bite that will keep you coming back bite after bite. It may look like a complicated dessert made by only the best chefs, but it's surprisingly easy to make! You just need some patience. The key to perfection is drying it out, which requires you to leave it in a (turned-off) oven overnight after it bakes.

If you’re looking for something a bit more festive, check out our Christmas wreath pavlova for a holiday spin on the classic.

Arrange a rack in the center of the oven; preheat to 300°. In a large bowl, beat egg whites with a large pinch of salt on medium-high speed with a handheld mixer (or in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment) until foamy, which should take about one minute.

According to recent reports, while beating, slowly add sugar and beat until meringue is thick and glossy, which should take about 7 minutes. Beat in vinegar, cornstarch, and vanilla until well combined.

Pile the meringue in the center of a parchment-lined baking sheet. Using a spatula or spoon, spread the mixture into an 8" circle. Make a small well in the center.

In a recent development, transfer to the oven, and immediately reduce the oven temperature to 250°. Bake the meringue until set but still white, which should take about an hour. Turn off the oven and let the pavlova cool completely in the oven for at least 2 hours and up to overnight. Transfer cooled pavlova to a platter.

Top with whipped cream and berries.

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

Store the unassembled pavlova in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2 days, keeping it away from humidity. Once topped with whipped cream and fresh fruit, refrigerate and enjoy within a day, as the meringue will soften over time.

Chili Crisp Yogurt Chicken

📅 20 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (418 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Epicurious

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that slather Greek yogurt and your favorite chili crisp on chicken thighs, roast in a hot oven, and you’ll be rewarded with juicy, tender meat with a delightful orange-tinged exterior.
  • More great chicken and rice recipes this way: One-Pot Chicken Thighs With Cilantro Rice and Beans; Spiced Coconut Chicken Rice; Nana’s Chicken and Rice Stew.
  • According to recent reports, preheat oven to 425°.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that slather Greek yogurt and your favorite chili crisp on chicken thighs, roast in a hot oven, and you’ll be rewarded with juicy, tender meat with a delightful orange-tinged exterior. But the best part of this sheet-pan dinner comes after the chicken is cooked: Spread cooked rice into the pan’s juices, then slide the baking sheet back into the oven. As the rice soaks up the deeply savory sauce, it will crisp in spots, creating a texture that’s somewhere between chewy-fluffy steamed grains and a freshly toasted pita chip. And when it comes to chili crisp, we love the iconic and easy-to-source Lao Gan Ma, but specialty brands like Fly By Jing are great too—just make sure the one you use is not too spicy, which will overpower the dish.

More great chicken and rice recipes this way: One-Pot Chicken Thighs With Cilantro Rice and Beans; Spiced Coconut Chicken Rice; Nana’s Chicken and Rice Stew.

According to recent reports, preheat oven to 425°. Season 6–8 skinless, boneless chicken thighs (1½–2 lb.) with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

Whisk together ¾ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt and ¼ cup plus 2 Tbsp. well-stirred chili crisp in a large bowl. Add chicken thighs and toss to coat.

Sources indicate that arrange chicken on a rimmed baking sheet and top with any yogurt mixture left in bowl. Bake chicken until deeply browned and an instant-read thermometer inserted into the thickest part of a thigh registers 165°, 25–30 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board or plate.

Spread 3 cups cooked jasmine or short-grain rice over baking sheet with chicken juices and bake until most of the juices have been absorbed and rice is starting to crisp in spots, 12–15 minutes.

Meanwhile, whisk together 1 Tbsp. finely grated lime zest, ¼ cup fresh lime juice, ½ tsp. sugar, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, and remaining ¼ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt in a small bowl.

In a recent development, combine ½ medium head of green cabbage (about 1 lb.), very thinly sliced, and a significant pinch of Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt in a large bowl. Using your hands, scrunch cabbage gently to soften. Add 1 small red onion, thinly sliced, 1 cup finely chopped cilantro, and yogurt dressing and toss to combine. Taste cabbage slaw and season with more salt if needed.

Slice chicken as desired and serve with crisped rice and cabbage slaw.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Seasonal travel is exciting, but getting everyone from point A to point B can be a production—especially when babies and pets are involved. Between navigating crowded airports, packing the car with what feels like half your house, and keeping your four-legged family members calm amid all the chaos, there’s a ton to think about. And while you can’t control flight delays, holiday traffic, or the timing of a much-needed diaper change, having the right travel gear can make a world of difference.

According to recent reports, enter Nuna and Tavo, two brands that bring thoughtful design, innovative safety features, and a beautiful aesthetic to (often hectic) family travel. Nuna’s premium baby gear helps take some of the stress out of everything from airport security to car-seat installations, while Tavo focuses the same level of attention on the safety and comfort of travel essentials designed specifically for pets. Think lightweight strollers that fold with one hand (because your other one is probably occupied), car seats that don’t require an online tutorial to install, and comfortable carriers that give your furry companions a safe spot of their own.

Whether you’re flying across the country to visit the grandparents, packing up for a holiday road trip, or exploring a newly introduced destination together, these six Nuna and Tavo essentials, available at Bloomingdale’s, can help make the journey a little more joyful for everyone involved.

Given crowded security lines, blowouts at the worst possible moment, and the sheer amount of stuff you have to tote, a lightweight stroller is a genuine lifesaver at the airport. At just 16.3 pounds, the Nuna VIAA cabn is designed to meet IATA cabin-size standards when folded with the armbar removed—though you’ll still want to double-check your airline’s requirements. One-handed steering makes navigating crowded terminals easier (especially when you’re juggling a much-needed iced coffee), while a roomy storage basket holds up to 22 pounds of diaper bags, coats, backup outfits, bottles, snacks, and approximately 47 things to keep your baby entertained. It even comes with a carrier bag for when it’s time to board.

In a recent development, this Nuna duo pairs the TRIV lx stroller, which folds with one hand and stands on its own, with the ultralight PIPA urbn infant car seat. And if you’ve ever broken a sweat or found yourself YouTubing car seat installation instructions for the 100th time, you’ll appreciate that this one clicks into place without a base, using its built-in pipaFIX rigid latch installation. Large rear wheels and all-wheel suspension pair with a spacious storage basket and handy tracking-device pocket to make the stroller ready for everyday outings.

It has been revealed that the Nuna SWIV’s standout feature is button-activated 360-degree rotation on all four wheels, allowing it to move sideways and pivot through tight spaces without the struggle of squeezing through crowded airport lines and store aisles that clearly weren’t designed with strollers in mind. A one-handed recline with three positions, including a near-flat option, makes adjustments easy, and the stroller is travel-system-ready with any Nuna PIPA series infant car seat, allowing you to move baby from the car to the stroller.

The Tavo Crispin gives your pet a roomy, comfortable spot of their own, with mesh panels for ventilation and visibility so they can still keep eyes on their humans. It’s impact-tested and secures to your vehicle using lower anchors and a top tether, with a protective memory-foam guard for added peace of mind. And when the holiday travels are over, it collapses for easy storage without taking up precious space at home.

Industry observers note that this Tavo travel system might be your fresh favorite on-the-road companion. The Maeve car seat attaches to the Roscoe Trek stroller frame, so you can go from the car to a festive outing without having to transfer your pup to a different carrier. All-terrain rear wheels and suspension make bumpy sidewalks easier to navigate, while one-touch brakes and a compact stroller fold come in handy when it’s time for a coffee stop or to load everything back into the car.

There’s a very particular type of heart-rate spike that comes with flying with a pet. You have to stand in the airline’s special-assistance line with your (probably nervous) dog or cat, only to finally reach the counter and hold your breath as the agent (and sometimes a supervisor) decides whether their carrier fulfills the rules. The Tavo Dupree II has a chic carry-on design that’s also crash-tested, complete with built-in vehicle connectors and a protective memory-foam guard. Mesh panels keep air circulating, while a trolley sleeve lets you slip it over your suitcase handle instead of carrying everything separately. You’ll still want to double-check your airline’s requirements before flying.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that listen, we all know that stuffing is the best part of Thanksgiving dinner, but because of the butter, eggs, and chicken broth that usually go into classic stuffing, it's a dish that vegans can't always enjoy—until now! We created a stuffing that's so delicious, you might even be convinced to make a few of your other holiday classics into vegan Thanksgiving versions.

Start your stuffing off by preheating the oven to 200° and slicing the bread into roughly 1” cubes. Spread the cubes in a single layer on a large baking sheet and bake for about 20 minutes, until the bread is nice and crisp.

Remove the bread from the oven and turn the temperature up to 350°. Grease a 13” x 9” baking dish with cooking spray and heat oil in a large skillet over medium heat. Add onion to the skillet and cook for about 5 minutes until lightly charred in some spots, then add the celery and garlic and continue to cook, stirring occasionally, until the celery starts to turn translucent. Pour in the vegetable stock and scrape up any browned bits—this is where all the flavor is. Season with salt and pepper.

Mix the bread cubes and chopped herbs in the vegetable stock mixture until well combined, then transfer to the prepared baking dish.

Industry observers note that cover the dish tightly with aluminum foil and place it in the oven to bake for 40 minutes. Carefully remove the foil and continue baking for another 35 minutes, until the stuffing is golden brown and crisp on top.

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

Looking for more vegan holiday inspo? Whip up our cauliflower stuffing for a low-carb option, or try out our vegetarian mushroom gravy or vegan mashed potatoes to truly complete your spread!

In a recent development, any leftovers can be stored in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 4 days. You can also prepare this dish ahead of time, as it’s the kind of dish that we think tastes even better after sitting for a day.

In a recent development, imagine a Parker House roll having a tryst with Asian-style milk bread and a classic French croissant—that’s the essence of salt bread, a.k.a. shio pan in Japan and sogeum-ppang in Korea.

“These little buns…they look so cute, but they are so rich,” guest contributor, and our deputy food editor, Hana Asbrink explains to BA Bake Club hosts Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic. “You can really just snack on them solo and be so satisfied.”.

Sources indicate that this month’s episode is also more bittersweet than usual, as Shilpa reveals that she is leaving Bon Appétit to take on new projects. “I’m so proud of Bake Club,” Shilpa says. “Thank you to all of our readers and listeners. You really have made this the most wholesome corner of the internet and my career.”.

We can’t let her go without a proper send off. Follow Shilpa on Instagram to see what comes next in her baking adventures. And fret not, BA Bake Club will continue full steam ahead with Jesse at the helm!

Tech Report: This Piping Hot Zenith Collaboration Explains the Future of the Watch Market

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1003 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In early July, I met with Zenith’s chief product officer Romain Marietta over Zoom to get a sneak peek at a watch that wouldn’t come out until November.
  • Industry observers note that zenith recently announced that it’s laying off roughly half of its current workforce as it attempts to shift its position in the market.
  • Lorel Monroy, a sales associate at LA’s Feldmar Watch Tech giant, tells me there’s “definitely been an uptick” in interest around Zenith this year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In early July, I met with Zenith’s chief product officer Romain Marietta over Zoom to get a sneak peek at a watch that wouldn’t come out until November. The latest Zenith G.F.J., made in partnership with the Los Angeles-based independent watchmaker J.N. Shapiro, is a gorgeous timepiece that combines the former’s mechanical know-how with Shapiro’s meticulously handmade dials. Over four months before the watch was even unveiled to the public, Marietta shared that 20 of the 25 pieces produced had already been sold. Of all the releases from the major Swiss brands in 2026, none better represent the future of luxury watchmaking than this high-end, fussily made, independent-adjacent, sold-out-before-you-ever-heard-about-it G.F.J.

Industry observers note that zenith recently announced that it’s laying off roughly half of its current workforce as it attempts to shift its position in the market. “All of us in our segment, which is described as mid-range, are going through a very difficult period,” Zenith CEO Benoit De Clerck told staff as he explained the restructuring, according to Le Temps. The brand has been shifting upmarket since last year, when it released a rainbow gem-set version of its flagship sport watch. The G.F.J. is the cornerstone of that new business. As the economy tilts even further in favor of the uber-rich, it’s also altering where the bulk of the profits come from for watchmakers. “Wealthy people are still wealthy, and even more wealthy,” Marietta noted. “It’s easier [now] to sell high-end watches than watches for 3,000 to 5,000 Swiss francs.”.

That’s true. Lorel Monroy, a sales associate at LA’s Feldmar Watch Tech giant, tells me there’s “definitely been an uptick” in interest around Zenith this year. Not for the brand’s flagship Chronomaster, which remains firmly in the starter luxury watch zone at $12,300, but for the far more expensive G.F.J., which starts at $49,900. “The luxury direction is the game changer,” Monroy said. Feldmar only received three G.F.J.s to allocate in 2026 and they were all promptly snapped up. There’s now a waitlist building at the retailer for the upscale model.

Recent findings suggest that when it comes to the G.F.J., Zenith has acted like MacGyver, finding endless uses for its smash-hit model. First released in the spring of 2025, the watch received two very pretty, well-received sequels earlier this year. In March, I got to test out the upcoming onyx-dial version for just a few hours before I had to send it along to Hollywood stylist Fabio Immediato, who promptly strapped it on Simu Liu’s wrist for the Oscars.

Industry observers note that over the summer, Zenith also launched this double-signed program, which allows the brand to work with independent makers like J.N. Shapiro. Before this latest release, the Swiss brand linked up with Japan’s beloved Naoya Hida.

Industry observers note that that watch was a fascinating representation of the project—the spotlessly clean dial was straight out of the latter’s workshop. Zenith, a historic brand backed by LVMH, ceded control entirely to the small Japanese indie. It was a massive success. To allocate the pieces, Marietta mentioned they narrowed the list to 10 clients, mainly from the Naoya Hida side, then sent an email that included the price tag of 60,000 Swiss francs but zero images of the watch. “They said yes right away, trusting us with the design,” Marietta said. “And that’s a great testimony of how the trust can be at that level when you buy a piece for [$75,000] without even seeing it, not even a picture.”.

In the topsy-turvy world of watches in 2026, it’s much sexier to be an independent brand than one in the stable of the world’s largest luxury conglomerate. Marietta calls the G.F.J. “an independent brand within our global lineup,” pointing to the high-level finishing and historic movement inside the piece—the type of nerdy details that appeal to the most seasoned collectors driving the industry. “The G.F.J. collection itself is bringing us newly introduced clients,” Marietta mentioned. “It's attracting clients who did not really have Zenith on their radar. These guys were more A. Lange & Söhne clients or with independents.”.

According to recent reports, zenith created irresistible bait for this fresh stripe of collectors. The new J.N. Shapiro-designed G.F.J. is absolutely gorgeous. The partners leverage the LA independent’s dedication to creating its dials by hand through a technique known as engine turning. I got to visit Shapiro’s workshop a few years ago and was charmed by the contrast of the brand’s cavernous industrial warehouse and the row of almost medieval-looking engine-turning machines lined up at the front of the room.

The dials of the new collaborative watches were painstakingly made on those very machines—on which a single mistake means tossing the whole thing in the bin—and then shipped off to Switzerland, where Zenith watchmakers installed them into cases. There are three different patterns on the dial, including a basketweave at the center and Shapiro’s signature invention, the Infinity Weave, inside the subdial. Much like on the Naoya Hida version, the dial is all Shapiro. Marietta notes, however, that it already resembles the brick pattern seen on the original G.F.J., which is based on the exterior of Zenith’s manufacture in Le Locle.

Zenith aims to release two collaborative versions of the G.F.J. annually moving forward. According to Marietta, a couple of years down the road, the brand may allow their indie partners to go beyond the dial and play with the case and movement as well.

According to recent reports, with the G.F.J., Zenith has created something that is tailor-made for today’s collectors. Seven-figure pieces are right now booming at auction, and it would take Moses himself to part the money flooding into the market right now. These deep-pocketed collectors are most interested in watches from independent makers: Auction houses have sold more million-dollar F.P. Journe watches this year than they have from either Rolex or Patek Philippe. As collectors search for the next hot watchmaker, they’re finding exactly what they’re looking for in a 161-year-old Swiss luxury brand.

According to recent reports, before Jennifer Lawrence volunteered as tribute on our screens, the story of Katniss Everdeen—and the world of Panem—first unfolded on the page. Suzanne Collins’s novel The Hunger Games quickly captivated readers everywhere in 2008, with its dystopian tale of a deadly competition among teenagers and the heroine who rose among them to defy the Capitol. The bestseller promptly evolved into a book trilogy and then a film series, and has since expanded into prequel novels and associated films.

Whether you are new to the series or looking to dive back in, you can find all five Hunger Games books below, listed chronologically by the events in Panem’s history rather than the year they were published.

As the first prequel in the series, The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes takes place during the tenth iteration of the Hunger Games. It follows 18-year-old Coriolanus Snow (the future President Snow) as he becomes a mentor for the games in an attempt to save his family from ruin. But the undertaking proves an unexpected challenge: He’s assigned a headstrong tribute from the lowly District 12, Lucy Gray Baird, and even though things get off to a rough start, they start developing feelings for each other. A film adaptation starring Rachel Zegler and Tom Blyth came out in 2023.

In a recent development, the newest novel in the series—also the second prequel—is set during the 50th Hunger Games, also known as a Quarter Quell year. This time, there are twice as many tributes in the arena as in a normal year. One of them is District 12 tribute Haymitch Abernathy—a beloved figure from The Hunger Games trilogy—who fears being taken away from his loved ones, including his sweetheart, Lenore Dove. Even with an understanding that he could fail, Haymitch is determined to fight and see the games through. The Sunrise on the Reaping film adaptation, starring Joseph Zada as Haymitch, was released in 2026.

The Hunger Games is the book that started it all. Technically the first entry in Collins’s series, the novel introduced readers to Panem, a dystopian nation located where North America once stood, with 12 distinct districts and a Capitol. To keep the districts in order, the Capitol hosts the annual Hunger Games, a televised competition in which teenage boys and girls from each district fight to the death. One of those players—a.k.a. tributes—is 16-year-old Katniss Everdeen, who takes the place of her younger sister and must do everything she can to survive.

Fresh off her Hunger Games win, Katniss Everdeen faces an upheaval in her relationship with Peeta Mellark, her fellow District 12 tribute, and confronts the growing ire of the Capitol. Displeased by the last-minute move that allowed both Katniss and Peeta to win the games, President Snow has informed Katniss she must do everything she can to staunch the growing rebellion amongst the districts. But with another Quarter Quell looming, Katniss understands the games have only just begun.

In a recent development, katniss is still standing, but at what cost? Her home is gone; the Capitol has captured Peeta; and a rebellion is underway in the districts. With the mysterious District 13 rising up to lead the revolution, Katniss must decide with whom her loyalties ultimately lie.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a Japanese-style rice porridge known as okayu. I ate this every morning in the early weeks of postpartum after my first daughter was born. It’s what our family reaches for whenever we need a simple, nourishing dish that warms from the inside out. For the smoothest porridge, let the rice soak in cold water before cooking.

It has been revealed that if you have time, soak the rice, which makes the texture softer and can aid in digestion. Place washed rice in a bowl and pour in water to cover by 1". Soak at least 30 minutes and up to 4 hours. Drain off excess water before starting the recipe. The wakame seaweed, which you’ve probably had in miso soup, can typically be found dried anywhere Asian groceries are available.

In The Fourth Trimester, we ask parents: What meal nourished you after welcoming your baby? This month it’s a cozy rice porridge by Eating at Home cookbook author Trinity Mouzon Wofford. Read more: Breakfast at Home, After Birth at Home.

Combine 1 cup short-grain rice, washed, soaked if desired, ¼ cup dried wakame (seaweed), 1 Tbsp. dried red shiso, and 6 cups low-sodium broth (any kind) or water in a large donabe, medium Dutch oven, or other heavy pot. Cover and bring to a boil over medium-high heat (you’ll hear bubbling). Uncover and stir, making sure nothing is stuck to bottom of pot. Cover and reduce heat to low. Continue to cook porridge 30 minutes more (resist the urge to peek).

According to recent reports, remove pot from heat and let porridge sit (still covered) 10 minutes. Uncover and stir. Rice grains should be cooked through, broken open, and creamy, but porridge should still be fairly loose. Season porridge with fine sea salt.

Ladle porridge into bowls and serve, topped with toasted sesame seeds, toasted sesame oil, and/or thinly sliced scallions.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“The area where I grew up, Belleville, is really different from the Hamptons,” mentioned Casablanca’s Charaf Tajer. “Growing up between Paris and Morocco, it seemed a very different landscape: it sounded very exotic to me.” Globalization might have shrunk the world—and flattened it too—but distance still creates room for the imagination to generate glamour. For this resort season Tajer projected his Casablanca formula on the Hamptons.

His starting point was a survey of Jackie Kennedy and the milieu of American East Coast society during the middle of the last century. The seaside estates, sailing boats, country clubs, and sprawling lawns of this privileged playground offered a newly introduced destination for a brand whose MO has always been rooted in a romanticized dislocation. “It’s kind of near the cities,” Tajer noted of the Hamptons, “but it has its own bubble.” Peering into that bubble through documentaries and archival imagery was an exercise in escapism, and Tajer intended this collection to be an escape route too. “It’s not that I don’t care: I’m really into the news. But I also feel like we need to care less, because the news can take us into a mental spiral.”.

Recent findings suggest that tajer presented the collection as the wardrobe of a dynastic clan on vacation, with each member bringing their own interpretation of American sportswear through a Casablanca-fied lens. Although shot in the UK, closer to Hertfordshire than the Hamptons, the images were cleverly set and staged. A scion crunched the gravel with a chunky laborador in a nicely homaged embroidered Skyliner jacket, wearing wide-leg chinos in one shot and skate shorts in another. Another lounged on a plump couch in seasonally-printed tennis gear, or lurked on the stairs in a camp collar shirt and embroidered wide-leg pants.

According to recent reports, the women wore striped knitted separates, scarf-print silks, and tennis dresses, as well as a long black knitted dress that offered a more universal option for evening. Throughout, the preppy and streetwear references were blended and sometimes distorted through color, proportion, and the prints and embroidered illustrations created by the brand’s three in-house artists.

The chinoiserie pattern adapted from a stately temple jar in this synthetic Camelot backdrop was prominently transposed into prints and patches. For Tajer, it served both as a hint toward a future project and as a reminder of how the decorative vernacular of one culture can become the status symbols of another.

In a recent development, tajer mentioned his ambition is to create a Casablanca wardrobe that can accommodate almost any occasion. The silk shirts that established the label have been joined by much more: This season’s additions included a leather tracksuit and upcoming hybrid driving/boat shoe. Tajer cited Ralph Lauren as an inspiration, saying: “This is always what I wanted to create with Casablanca: a full, cohesive world.”.

The Best Cast-Iron Skillets for a Lifetime of Cooking (2026)

📅 16 Jun 2021 | ⏱️ 22 min read (4324 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that to these two camps of people I say: “I don’t want to fight you, and I already know why you feel the way you feel.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that for some people there isn’t much of a debate around who makes the best cast-iron skillet. There is a die-hard fan base loyal to the affordable US-made Lodge cast-iron pan that will not hear of any other suggestions.

There are others (cast-iron nerds and collectors) who swear by the superior quality of their vintage pan from Griswold or Wagner that they found at a scrap yard, de-rusted in a bucket with a DIY electrolysis setup, and seasoned with a proprietary oil blend in the furnaces of their bespoke restoration workshop.

Recent findings suggest that to these two camps of people I say: “I don’t want to fight you, and I already know why you feel the way you feel. Please do not send me any angry emails.”.

Industry observers note that if you’ve been loyal to your own cast-iron pan for years—or decades—I don’t expect to change your mind. My goal is merely to provide recommendations for cast-iron cookware based on side-by-side testing and the input collectively provided by members of our staff. Agree with me and my team or don’t; either way, I’m happy if people are passionate about cooking with cast iron because I too enjoy it a great deal.

In a recent development, cast-iron frying pans were the original nonstick pans, before ceramic nonstick and PTFE rolled around, and unlike modern nonstick coatings, a cast-iron pan’s surface actually gets more nonstick over time rather than degrading week by week. This is because, through continued cooking, thin layers of oil polymerize to the surface of the pan, creating a glassy nonstick surface that improves with continued use. They are also strong enough to handle metal utensils. The same can’t be stated for that Instagram-famous nonstick pan (you know the one).

Industry observers note that yes, there are ways you can damage this seasoning layer, but these pans are far more resilient than lots of people think, and they aren’t actually all that difficult to care for. Talk to cast-iron enthusiasts and they’ll tell you the best way to season a cast-iron skillet is to just keep cooking with it.

Recent findings suggest that and cook with it you can. Cast-iron pans are amazing for fried eggs, skillet hashes, cornbread, and sautéed greens. At a high heat, they do an incredible job searing strip steaks, London broil, and chicken thighs, giving you a burnished crispy exterior.

Bottom line, cast-iron cooking is an absolute joy, and every kitchen tool kit should include some cast iron alongside its stainless-steel and carbon steel pans and enameled Dutch oven.

Upcoming in this update: A review of Made In's new cast-iron pan as well as more long-term testing information for our winner.

Size(s): 10.5" (4.5 lb.), 12" (6 lb.), 13.5" (7.5 lb.)Pre-seasoned: Yes.

Industry observers note that what I loved: Because they’re much more expensive than the Lodges folks got used to, many feel a certain type of way about the upcoming era of smooth, vintage-style cast-iron pans that includes this Lancaster. But when you have the opportunity to test a bunch of these pans side by side, you really get a sense of their differences (however small), and you’d be surprised by the things you notice. It was in this apples-to-apples testing that this pan, manufactured by a small company based in Southeastern Pennsylvania, really set itself apart.

In a recent development, the Lancaster is the lightest cast-iron pan I’ve tested, weighing in at 4 lb. for the No. 8 (10"-diameter) pan. Most cast-iron pans of a similar size are around 5 lb. or more—a seemingly small difference in number that makes a surprisingly big difference in hand. When laid out next to a dozen pans in the Test Kitchen, multiple testers singled out this pan as being the most comfortable to hold and maneuver.

Sources indicate that it has thinner walls than a typical cast-iron skillet, which allows it to heat up faster. In testing, it came to temp over one minute faster than pans with thicker walls. We were concerned this would mean a reduction in the level of heat retention you’d want to crisp up the edges of some skillet cornbread, but we didn’t find that to be a problem at all. The cooking surface also demonstrated relatively even heat for a cast-iron pan (you really can’t expect too much from cast iron, though; cold spots are sort of inevitable with the material).

The pan comes pre-seasoned, but as is the case with most smooth cast-iron pans, this seasoning layer isn’t nearly as robust as what you’d find on a conventional Lodge or Victoria pan. The polished surface does aid in the pan’s nonstick properties, though, so we found the pan was exceptionally nonstick right out of the box.

It has been revealed that other testing sites have criticized this style of smooth cast-iron pan for getting stained after cooking, but to that we say: This is the process of seasoning developing on the pan. That staining is a feature, not a bug.

An earlier design of this pan didn’t include a helper handle, a feature we missed but forgave because the pan was already so easy to wield. However, Lancaster recently updated the design to include one—all the better in our book. Check out my full review of the Lancaster No. 8 here.

What I’d leave: The main drawback here is the cost. This pan will set you back $175, a steep price for cookware with a reputation for being budget-friendly. I’ll just say this: People happily pay comparable prices for nonstick ceramic cookware that lasts only a year or two at best. This pan, provided you don’t drop it in an industrial crucible, will last a lifetime.

Sources indicate that in the long run: I have more patience than a lot of people when it comes to taking care of pans. So I will concede that the out of the box seasoning isn’t that robust. Some tasks, like searing off meat, can strip the seasoning slightly at first. With the Lancaster, I’ve found that this doesn’t impact the pans overall nonstick-ness. It does, however, mean you have to keep an eye out for rust until it gets a couple uses under its belt.

According to recent reports, below you’ll see two Lancaster pans. The left is four years old and the right is fresh from the box (you can tell because the earlier generation of pans didn’t have the helper handle). These are the pans after searing off two chicken thighs. You can see how the pan on the left has a robust, established seasoning, while the one on the right has some gray patches where the chicken skin pulled off some of that seasoning. From experience (I am the owner of the pan on the left), I can say that all you really need to do is keep cooking with it to get that seasoning back, but if you want to do a whole round of seasoning in the oven yourself, it certainly won’t hurt. Honestly, had I just sautéed some onions in the rendered schmaltz after cooking the chicken, those spots would be taken care of.

For comparison, I seared some chicken thighs in both pans. The factory seasoning might get patchy after the first use. Don’t let that scare you, just keep cooking with it. If you’re really worried about rust, just wipe down the surface of the pan with a tiny bit of neutral oil, buff off the excess, and put it over the heat for a few minutes.

It has been revealed that some people complain about the cosmetic changes to these smooth pans when breaking them in To reiterate: It does not impact the performance of the pan. If it bothers you, I encourage you to think about how it’s a record of use and proof that it’s growing and developing alongside you. Or, if you’re just an unsentimental aesthete, perhaps read up on the concept of wabi-sabi. I personally think that my pan is the most beautiful piece of cookware I own!

If you want a high-quality pan that’s not only a pleasure to cook with, but can serve as a family heirloom for generations to come, consider this one. If you’re just looking for a workhorse that won’t break the bank, go for the budget option below.

Size(s): 4.8" (1.1 lb.), 6.5" (2 lb.), 8" (3.1 lb.), 10" (5.5 lb.), 12" (7.5 lb.)Pre-seasoned: Yes.

According to recent reports, what I loved: Again, I apologize for snubbing Lodge, as even in our office we have a number of staunch brand loyalists. But in my testing, the Victoria edged out the fan favorite on two separate metrics. Victoria pans are pre-seasoned with flaxseed oil and arrive glossy and exceptionally nonstick. Having a more thorough pre-seasoning is more key on cast-iron pans, as they are prone to sticking early on. We found the Victoria pan’s factory seasoning slicker than Lodge’s, which made frying potatoes and eggs ever so slightly easier. Do all cast-iron seasonings improve with continued use over time? Yes. But we know that some people want as much of a head start as they can get, and this pan offers you the best one.

The other way the Victoria bested the Lodge is in its form factor. The pour spouts on the Victoria are nice and wide, making it easy to pour off oil or other pan juices, and testers found the handle shape slightly more comfortable than the Lodge.

I’ll be honest, though, these differences are pretty small, and if you feel drawn to the Lodge name, I recommend it as well.

In a recent development, what I’d leave: Given it’s bargain pricing, there isn’t much to dislike here. I will note this pan is significantly heavier than the Lancaster pan—a full pound and a half for the same diameter skillet. Heavier skillets are cheaper and easier to produce, so it’s a trade-off you’ll have to accept if you want a less expensive piece of cookware.

According to recent reports, 1. We had several members of staff handle the pans to get a broad sense of how easy the pans were to maneuver. Then we got to cooking.

2. Using a little bit of oil, we fried eggs sunny-side up and scrambled to see how much (if anything) stuck to the pan.

In a recent development, 3. We seared skin-on chicken thighs to get a sense of how evenly heat was distributed around the cooking surface. We also measured how long it took for the pan to reach 375° at medium heat.

4. We washed the pans in hot water, noting any places where seasoning might have worn away.

5. We re-seasoned the pans ourselves in an oven for an hour at 500°.

6. We cooked another round of eggs to observe any changes.

I omitted enameled cast-iron skillets like those made by Le Creuset or Staub because enameled surfaces offer a different experience in terms of both cooking and care. I also chose to exclude any cast-iron griddles or grill pans since they are too different functionally.

Sizing is a bit different from organization to company, but I chose to stick with a 10"-diameter skillet—a No. 8 in traditional cast-iron sizing—as it is the most common size available.

How nonstick is the pan out of the box?

Industry observers note that I should clarify that cast-iron pans aren’t nonstick in the sense that you can cook an egg in the pan without any oil and slide it around. A really well-seasoned pan that’s a glossy lacquered black from years of use might get close, but the seasoning really just helps food release more easily from the pan—and the more seasoning there is, the less oil you’ll need for food to release.

Sources indicate that I evaluated the pans on their out-of-the-box factory seasoning, because having a solid seasoning layer to start with diminishes the amount of time you need to break in a pan. This matters more with cheaper, rough textured cast iron, which is more prone to sticking when it lacks proper seasoning. For polished or vintage-style cast-iron pans (like the Lancaster), factory seasoning is nice, but the smooth surface also aids in preventing sticking, so it isn’t as crucial in the beginning stages of using the pan. That is why, throughout this review you see more emphasis on factory seasoning when discussing budget pans.

Is the pan designed in a way that makes it easy to use?

Industry observers note that I counted form and design heavily in how I judged these pans. I wanted the pan to be comfortable and easy to maneuver, so I looked for pans that were lightweight (relatively, we’re talking about iron here) and had handles that were comfortable to grip. If the pan was heavier, I wanted a helper handle for moving it from the cooktop to the oven. I didn’t place an emphasis on whether handle was designed to stay cool, because even a handle billed as “stay cool” will get dangerously hot when cooking for long enough, so I feel it’s better to just make a habit of always using an oven mitt or cloth to grab a cast-iron handle.

According to recent reports, heavy-duty, even-heating, satisfyingly weighty skillets are staples in the BA Test Kitchen because of their versatility. Stainless-steel and carbon steel frying pans get hot quickly, but they don’t always have the heat-retention capabilities of cast iron. And while nonstick pans are nice for scrambled eggs and crispy-skinned fish, many are not oven-safe and should never be exposed to high temperatures, so you can’t sear safely with them.

Stargazer Cast Iron Skillet - 10.5".

In a recent development, the Stargazer is a lovely pan. Like the Lancaster, its a vintage-style skillet, so it has a smooth texture that’s easy to clean. The surface develops seasoning well, and the curved lip allows for easy pouring at any angle. Ultimately, it is one of the heavier high-end skillets available on the market, which is why we don’t have it as a winner. However, if weight isn’t a huge concern for you, it is still an excellent pan.

Recent findings suggest that if you know cast-iron pans, you might see the Yeti cast-iron skillet and might find that it looks somewhat familiar. This is because Yeti acquired cult-favorite Butter Pat several years ago. The Yeti skillet is just the Butter Pat by a newly introduced name, and apart from the logo, the finish, handle shape, and overall design remain unchanged. This pan has a nice velvety surface that holds on to seasoning very well, while still maintaining a smooth, glossier finish that makes vintage-style pans so desirable. Small gripes: The handle design wasn’t a favorite among testers, and the side walls are a slightly shorter than most other cast-iron pans. It’s also a touch heavier and a couple touches more expensive than our winner. Still, this is an excellent cast-iron pan and makes a great family heirloom.

Lodge Cast-Iron Skillet with Red Mini Silicone Hot Handle Holder, 8".

People who track recommendations like these tend to be shocked that we don’t place the Lodge as our winner or budget pick. It is a fantastic pan, make no mistake. It has a great factory seasoning that’s resilient from the jump, and the 10" costs around twenty bucks—so what gives? When it came down to it, the Victoria pan had a slicker factory seasoning out of the box and a more comfortable handle design.

Smithey No. 10 Cast-Iron Skillet.

Recent findings suggest that another high-end polished cast-iron pan on the list. Smithey pans are gorgeous, so much so that it almost feels wrong cooking with them. However, you should cook with it straight away, as the factory seasoning is a little light on these, and we observed a little bit wearing away after the first couple rounds of cooking prior to us adding an additional layer of seasoning. Senior editor Noah Kaufman has been cooking with the Smithey multiple times a week for a couple years and indicates that within a few months of regular use and two bouts of seasoning in the oven he no longer worried about stuck eggs or steaks.

Gorgeous as they are, Smithey pans are heavy, though, at 5.8 lb. for the 10" skillet.

Industry observers note that this skillet is the second lightest (4.3 lb. at 10") and has a velvety surface that holds on to seasoning a little better than the smooth polished pans. Like the Stargazer, it also has a curved lip instead of a pour spout, but I found that this pan does have a bit of a dribbling problem, which I wasn't crazy about. Still, one member of our team who has now lived with this pan for years loves it and uses it every day.

Lodge Cast-Iron Blacklock Skillet, Triple Seasoned - 10.25".

Lodge released this pan in response to the wave of newly introduced and fancy polished pans, and as beautiful (quite beautiful), well-seasoned (three glossy layers), and lightweight as it is (almost even with the Lancaster), our testers found the handle uncomfortable to hold.

In a recent development, ooni is a pizza oven firm, and this pan is really designed for cooking in an oven rather than on the stovetop. It has a detachable handle, which is actually a genius bit of design that makes it easy and comfortable to grab out of a blazing hot pizza oven. But the sides are too shallow for doing more normal cast-iron things like frying chicken or sautéing greens. It is, however, great for cornbread and pizookies.

According to recent reports, this is Made In’s official entry into the cast-iron new wave. The pan has a smooth machined surface, nice design touches, like curved sidewalls and a spacious helper handle. The primary handle is nice to hold; however, a longer handle can make a pan feel heavier and add strain on the wrists. This pan is not the lightest, either. I found it difficult to transport the full pan from the stovetop to the oven using only one hand, so consider this a pan for people with meaty forearms. Made In also uses flaxseed oil for the factory seasoning, which is a controversial choice in the cast-iron world. The reason for that controversy is that, while the finish flaxseed oil produces is glossy and attractive, it tends to be brittle. Especially with newer pans, a flaxseed seasoning has a tendency to wear away with regular cooking. After testing, I did notice this pan had some gray (unseasoned) patches after a round of searing meat. Again, not a big deal—just keep cooking with it— but something to keep in mind. All of that being remarked, I do still think this is a high-quality pan. During the cooking tests, I had absolutely no concerns with sticking whatsoever.

This pan is pretty similar to a standard Lodge or Victoria, but with a seasoning that’s not as nonstick out of the box. We did find, however, that it added latest layers of seasoning quite well.

Valor Pre-seasoned Cast-Iron Skillet.

In a recent development, the Valor is apparently a favorite in restaurants, but there’s nothing special to it that makes it stand out. If anything, the pour spouts are so small they might as well not be there at all.

In a recent development, we’re all for innovation, which is what Finex sought to do with its octagonal pan and its bulbous handle, but we didn’t really observe any value from the modifications. While the octagonal shape is easier for flipping you could just use a bigger cast-iron pan for anything you want to flip. And its “speed cool” handle was awkward to hold.

Anytime KitchenAid ventures beyond the small appliance space you never quite know what you’re gonna get. In this case, it’s a cast-iron pan that is totally average in every way, except for its minimalist modern design. We think this pan is too expensive for what you’re getting.

Industry observers note that “Ooh, a lid!” Was the universal reaction to this cast-iron pan. If you like the idea of having a lid for your pan, then this is your pan. The problem with cast-iron lids, though, is that they don’t benefit from the progressive seasoning development the rest of the pan gets as you cook with it. Lids are only really dealing with evaporative moisture, which makes them even more likely to rust. Smithey, up above, sells glass lids that fit their pans, which, while not as oven-safe, won’t have that rust problem.

According to recent reports, this is Victoria’s answer to the high-end polished cast-iron pan. The seasoning is great, but the pan is heavier than the Lancaster, and we didn’t love all the extra design embellishments. The brass insert on the handle had no practical value (it heated up quicker than the surrounding cast iron). Also, all the extra ridges and divots just meant more places for gunk to get stuck in.

Amazon customers really like this pan. It comes with a silicone handle cover and a glass lid, which is nice (glass is a better material for a lid than cast iron). It also has tall 3" sides that make this pan great for frying. Beyond that, though, the pan is heavy and seemed to be barely pre-seasoned.

This is a super polished cast-iron pan with a glossy cooking surface that was nice to work with. However, we noticed quite a few cosmetic issues, like small nicks and rough edges that made it seem like there were some corners cut in the manufacturing process.

According to recent reports, another pan that is just fine. The factory seasoning is minimal, so you’ll have to build that up yourself. There are several better options that are just as affordable from Victoria, Lodge, and others.

This is an affordable pan that looks a lot like a Lodge, but with a lesser factory seasoning.

Amazon Basics Pre-seasoned Cast-Iron Pan.

The seasoning that came on this pan out of the box was pretty bad, and with so many other cheap alternatives that offer much better quality, we don’t see the point in purchasing this pan. It’s also only available in a 15" diameter at the time of writing, which is bigger (and heavier) than most people need.

Industry observers note that when you first get your pan, you’ll want to season it. We recommend this even when the pan comes labeled as pre-seasoned. To do this, just lightly rub a bone-dry pan with a thin layer of high-heat neutral vegetable oil and place it upside down in a very hot oven—450°F–500°F should do the trick. Leave for an hour, turn off the heat, let it cool completely in the oven (you should be able to take it out without an oven mitt or towel), rub with a tiny bit more oil, and store. You can season cast iron as many times as you’d like to build up a glossy nonstick surface; when the pan looks dull or dry, it’s time to moisturize.

Industry observers note that no, you can’t chuck it in the dishwasher, and you won’t be using your normal hand-wash methods, but a cast-iron skillet really doesn’t require much love. When it’s time to clean up, simply wipe a damp rag across the surface of your pan, then dry it thoroughly. Often, that’ll be enough. But if there are any crusty bits, try pouring coarse salt in there and going at it with a Tawashi scrubber, which has soft bristles that whisk away any detritus. Many will tell you to avoid soap at all costs lest you ruin your careful seasoning, but a little dish soap is fine—just don’t let it sit in hot water. (Read our complete guide to cleaning cast iron.).

For really baked on crumbs, try The Ringer, a handy chain mail scrubber that easily rinses clean between uses. After cleaning your cast iron, be sure to wipe your fry pan very dry—this is key for preventing any rust spots. Then take a teeny bit of neutral cooking oil (like canola or vegetable), smear on a paper towel, and give it a light coating. Take care to get the handle and the bottom as well as the cooking surface, as rust can crop up anywhere. And you’re good to go! It sounds involved, but it really only takes a few minutes. A well-seasoned pan takes virtually no time at all, so dutifully season and you’ll be rewarded.

Tossed your skillet in the sink absentmindedly or left it out in the rain only to find it’s developed a layer of orange rust? Don’t panic—rusting can happen pretty easily if you allow your pan to come into contact with water for an extended period of time (it is made of iron, after all). But that doesn’t mean it’s ruined. A salt scrub will help with most small spots, while a vinegar soak is the cure for more serious cases. (Read more on dealing with pesky cast-iron rust patches.).

If, after all of that, you’re still intimidated by raw cast-iron cookware, you might want to consider an enameled cast-iron skillet. It offers all of the heat retention and distribution of a well-seasoned cast-iron pan, plus it has a porcelain enamel to prevent rusting. Unlike a Le Creuset Dutch oven, enameled cast-iron skillets, like Staub’s, have a dark textured enamel that helps with browning and crisping.

Recent findings suggest that wilder Davies: I have been Epicurious and Bon Appétit’s resident cookware tester and researcher for over six years. I have cooked with hundreds and hundreds of pans and have asked chefs, materials scientists, and manufacturers far too many questions about things that go clank in the kitchen. I am a big apologist of nonstick alternatives, and strongly believe in a buy-it-for-life ethos when it comes to outfitting your pantry.

Apple Juice Bread

📅 22 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (716 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Epicurious

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A simple swap from water to apple juice transforms this basic bread recipe into a subtly sweet loaf that is perfect to tear into at breakfast time with a smear of good butter on top, but it also takes a PB&J to the next level.
  • According to recent reports, I first encountered the idea at the small four-seat teppanyaki restaurant in the back of the Suiran Hotel in Kyoto, Japan, where chef Tsubasa Yamaguchi served it before my first course; it was a perfect way to start the meal.
  • Recent findings suggest that take care when you’re lowering the bread into the Dutch oven; it is a slightly nerve-wracking moment but a little attention is all that’s needed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A simple swap from water to apple juice transforms this basic bread recipe into a subtly sweet loaf that is perfect to tear into at breakfast time with a smear of good butter on top, but it also takes a PB&J to the next level. The subtle, but unmistakable, undercurrent of apple sweetness struck me as a bit of a magic trick in a bread that, otherwise, to the eye and hand was just a soft white loaf.

According to recent reports, I first encountered the idea at the small four-seat teppanyaki restaurant in the back of the Suiran Hotel in Kyoto, Japan, where chef Tsubasa Yamaguchi served it before my first course; it was a perfect way to start the meal. When I asked him what he did differently to prepare it, he mentioned he just took the same rustic bread recipe he baked elsewhere and used apple juice in place of water. I was incredulous. That was it? The same amount? The same technique? Yes and yes, he said. I was hooked. It turns out the water-to-juice switcheroo gives an added taste of fall without taking anything away from the shape and texture. It’s become an instant favorite at my house both breakfast and lunch, and I expect it will be at yours.

Recent findings suggest that take care when you’re lowering the bread into the Dutch oven; it is a slightly nerve-wracking moment but a little attention is all that’s needed. You can do it!

More apple recipes here: 37 Apple Desserts That Make Us Want to Pick the Whole Orchard.

Mix 4 cups (500 g) all-purpose flour, 1¾ cups apple juice, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 Tbsp. sugar, and one ¼-oz. envelope instant yeast (about 2¼ tsp.) in a large bowl just until flour is hydrated and a very shaggy dough forms, about 1 minute. Cover bowl with plastic wrap and let dough sit at room temperature 15 minutes.

Set a small bowl of room-temperature water on work surface for easy reaching. Uncover dough, dip your hand in water and stretch one side of dough up and over to meet opposite side; turn bowl 90°. Repeat 3 more times, turning bowl 90° after each fold. (This constitutes 1 full fold.) If dough doesn’t always stretch to meet opposite side, just aim for the middle. Wet your hands and shake off excess water any time dough begins to feel sticky. Cover dough and let sit 30 minutes (set a timer). Repeat folding process to make 1 full fold. Re-cover and let dough sit another 30 minutes. Repeat folding process and resting one more time. By the last fold, dough should be significantly smoother and tighter.

Transfer dough to a generously floured surface, dust with flour, and shape into a tight ball. Dust dough with more flour. Dust a kitchen towel with flour and place inside a high-sided bowl to line. Arrange dough, seam side up, in bowl on top of towel. Tightly cover bowl with plastic wrap and let dough sit in a warm spot until puffy, about 45 minutes.

According to recent reports, place a rack in middle of oven, then set a large ovenproof Dutch oven with a lid on it; preheat oven to 400°. Place a 12" square of parchment paper on a flat surface. Cut a 2"-long slit in each corner toward the center. Very carefully, tip dough out onto center of parchment, trying your best not to deflate it or ruin its shape. (It’s easiest to place parchment on a flat plate so you can easily turn dough out of bowl.) Working very quickly and using a pair of kitchen shears lightly coated in vegetable oil, cut an X in center of bread. Remove pot from oven and very carefully lower dough into pot. Cover pot and return to oven.

Sources indicate that bake bread 35 minutes. Uncover pot, reduce oven temperature to 375°, and continue to bake bread until crust is deeply browned, 35–40 minutes more. Carefully tip loaf out onto a wire rack and let cool at least 1 hour before slicing.

Industry observers note that do Ahead: Bread can be baked 3 days ahead. Let cool completely; store airtight at room temperature.

Why Peptide Skincare Might Actually Be Worth Your While, According to Experts

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1057 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the recent buzz around peptides came to a head last month when U.S.
  • “I’ve had a lot of patients come in since the HHS ruling,” indicates Erik Peterson, MD, a board-certified dermatologist in Latest York City, who likens the recent policy change to “opening the floodgates,” resulting in a surge of interest—particularly from patients who’ve come across claims of peptide-based skincare being like ‘botox in a bottle.’.
  • Recent findings suggest that “It’s interesting how they are suddenly so popular, because peptides have been around for like 30 years in skincare,” states Malika Sloan, medical esthetician and founder of Sloan Studio in Upcoming York City.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the recent buzz around peptides came to a head last month when U.S. Secretary of Health and Human Services (HHS) Robert F. Kennedy Jr. revealed that six unregulated injectables, including the highly controversial “Wolverine stack” BPC-157 and TB-500, will now be available for broad use throughout the United States. Meanwhile, unsurprising to derms and estheticians everywhere, the rising tide of interest in peptides has spilled over into skincare, where the molecules have long served as an active ingredient.

“I’ve had a lot of patients come in since the HHS ruling,” indicates Erik Peterson, MD, a board-certified dermatologist in Latest York City, who likens the recent policy change to “opening the floodgates,” resulting in a surge of interest—particularly from patients who’ve come across claims of peptide-based skincare being like ‘botox in a bottle.’.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s interesting how they are suddenly so popular, because peptides have been around for like 30 years in skincare,” states Malika Sloan, medical esthetician and founder of Sloan Studio in Upcoming York City. “They’ve been incorporated into cosmetic formulations for decades, with ingredients like matrixyl helping to popularize them in the early 2000s. What’s exciting now is how much more sophisticated the formulations have become.”.

If you’re curious about peptide-based skincare products—what they potentially can do, what they definitely cannot—and which products experts recommend for the best results, here’s everything you need to know.

Recent findings suggest that peptides, regardless of whether they’re injected via syringe or applied topically with a serum or cream, are short chains of amino acids that instruct your body to execute specific functions. Insulin, for example, is a peptide that helps the body regulate blood sugar, and it’s been in use since the 1920s. More recently, GLP-1 drugs (short for glucagon-like peptide-1) have been found to curb food cravings and slow stomach emptying, making them highly effective for weight loss. The list of uses for peptides is virtually endless, ranging from muscle growth and wound healing to balancing hormones and managing inflammation.

According to recent reports, in skincare, topical peptides work much the same way as their injectable counterparts, but on a more localized level, directing your skin to carry out specific functions, “the first of which tends to be increasing production of collagen and elastin, which are two of the major determinants of skin quality,” says Dr. Peterson. They’ve also been shown to help even out skin tone, repair the skin barrier, and reduce the appearance of fine lines and wrinkles.

Recent findings suggest that the world of peptides is still a bit of a Wild West. A quick Google search for peptide skincare will yield dozens of results for unresearched compounds promising you flawless skin. And then, of course, there are the influencers. “You see all these kids on TikTok who are talking about their beauty routines, and they’re like 19 years old,” indicates Peterson. “It’s like, ‘Amazing, your skin obviously looks great, because you’re a child.’” In reality, the list of peptides that you can truly depend on to move the needle (without an actual needle) is surprisingly short, at least until more research is done.

According to recent reports, “The two peptides that are out right now that have any sort of viable data on them are palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 and GHK-Cu,” says Peterson. Signaling peptides, as they’re called—such as palmitoyl pentapeptide-4, better known as matrixyl—have some of the strongest clinical and anecdotal evidence for stimulating collagen and reducing the appearance of wrinkles. Although, as Peterson points out, much of the scientific data has been industry funded, “so we always have to be a bit skeptical.”.

Industry observers note that carrier peptides—like GHK-Cu, a popular copper peptide—on the other hand, “have some good lab data, but very minimal human data,” Peterson says. Nonetheless, products containing GHK-Cu are widely heralded for their ability to repair damaged tissue, reduce inflammation, and stimulate production of collagen and elastin. “I find copper peptides particularly interesting because of the research surrounding tissue repair and collagen-related remodeling pathways,” says Sloan.

In a recent development, as for acetyl hexapeptide-8, or argireline, as it’s more commonly known—aka “botox in a bottle”—don’t waste your money. “From a physiological perspective, it can’t possibly work,” notes Peterson, who explains that the molecules of this particular peptide are simply too large to pass through the surface of the skin. He compares it to skincare products that contain collagen rather than spur the body to produce its own. “Collagen is a massive molecule,” he says. “It would be like putting cow’s milk on your face—it’s not going to do anything.” Sure enough, a 2023 study found the effects of topical argireline to be “not statistically significant.”.

Sources indicate that instead, for those looking for the most noticeable results, Sloan recommends seeking out products that combine proven peptides with complementary, similarly validated ingredients—like SkinCeuticals’ P-TIOX Anti-Wrinkle Peptide Cream. “I like that the cream also incorporates ceramides, niacinamide, and moisturizing ingredients, making it an interesting option for someone looking to address both hydration and visible signs of aging,” she says. Peterson’s pick, The Rich Cream from Augustinus Bader, flanks signaling peptides with hyaluronic acid and vitamin E to improve moisture retention and bolster the skin’s protective barrier.

Peptides are a relatively low-maintenance addition to most skin regimens. “One of the reasons I love incorporating peptides into at-home skincare is that they’re generally well tolerated and relatively easy to combine with other ingredients,” indicates Sloan, who notes that peptides can typically be used alongside other popular actives like vitamin C, niacinamide, hyaluronic acid, and retinoids. “I typically recommend incorporating a peptide serum after cleansing and before moisturizer,” she says.

Just keep in mind that peptides alone won’t take the place of a well-rounded skincare regimen. “The best, most robust data still comes from the tried-and-true favorites of all dermatologists—protecting your collagen with consistent sunscreen use, and the best signaling molecule of them all: topical retinoids,” Peterson states.

It has been revealed that and, of course, don’t expect overnight results—despite what social media might have you believe. “Peptides are just signals for your skin, not magic in a bottle,” Peterson says. “The few studies that there are show at least three months of consistent usage before results are seen, so stick it out if you want to give it a real try.”.
